claim: Status epilepticus (SE) is a common neurological emergency for which new treatments are needed.
source: Status epilepticus (SE) is a common neurological emergency for which new treatments are needed.
evidence: This is a general statement about the clinical need for new SE treatments, supported by established medical knowledge.

claim: Systemic administration of an aromatase inhibitor after seizure onset strongly suppresses both electrographic and behavioral seizures induced by kainic acid (KA) in rats.
source: Here, we show in rats that systemic administration of an aromatase (estrogen synthase) inhibitor after seizure onset strongly suppresses both electrographic and behavioral seizures induced by kainic acid (KA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2 showing effects of fadrozole on seizures.

claim: KA-induced SE stimulates synthesis of estradiol (E2) in the hippocampus.
source: We found that KA-induced SE stimulates synthesis of estradiol (E2) in the hippocampus, a brain region commonly involved in seizures and where E2 is known to acutely promote neural activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data presented in Figure 4 showing increased hippocampal E2 levels after KA.

claim: Hippocampal E2 levels were higher in rats experiencing more severe seizures.
source: Hippocampal E2 levels were higher in rats experiencing more severe seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 4 showing correlation between seizure severity and E2 levels.

claim: Intra-hippocampal aromatase inhibition suppressed seizures.
source: Consistent with a seizure-promoting effect of hippocampal estrogen synthesis, intra-hippocampal aromatase inhibition also suppressed seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6 showing effects of intra-hippocampal fadrozole.

claim: Approximately one-third of SE cases are refractory to first line (benzodiazepine) and second line (anti-epileptic drug) treatments.
source: ~One-third of SE cases are refractory to first line (benzodiazepine) and second line (anti-epileptic drug) treatments, and often require pharmacologically induced coma to control seizures (Novy et al., 2010; Betjemann and Lowenstein, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The overall mortality rate of SE is estimated at 20%.
source: The overall mortality rate of SE is estimated at 20% (DeLorenzo et al., 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Patients who recover from SE have an increased likelihood of subsequent unprovoked seizures.
source: patients who recover have an increased likelihood of subsequent unprovoked seizures (Hesdorffer et al., 1998; Holtkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Estrogens are proconvulsant in animal models.
source: Estrogens have long been known to be proconvulsant, both in animal models (Terasawa and Timiras, 1968; Nicoletti et al., 1985; Buterbaugh and Hudson, 1991; Edwards et al., 1999; Woolley, 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Estrogens are proconvulsant in human patients.
source: Estrogens have long been known to be proconvulsant, both in animal models (Terasawa and Timiras, 1968; Nicoletti et al., 1985; Buterbaugh and Hudson, 1991; Edwards et al., 1999; Woolley, 2000) and in human patients (Bäckström, 1976; Herzog et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The hippocampus of both sexes contains enzymatic machinery to synthesize estrogens, including 17β-estradiol (E2).
source: The hippocampus of both sexes contains enzymatic machinery to synthesize estrogens, including 17β-estradiol (E2) (Hojo et al., 2004; Kretz et al., 2004; Tabatadze et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The hippocampus can synthesize E2 in vitro.
source: studies in primary hippocampal cultures (Prange-Kiel et al., 2003), slice cultures (Kretz et al., 2004) and acute slices (Hojo et al., 2004) show that the hippocampus can synthesize E2 in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 levels in hippocampal slices were increased by 30 min of NMDA treatment.
source: In hippocampal slices, E2 levels were increased by 30 min of NMDA treatment (Hojo et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: E2 applied to hippocampal slices increases neuronal excitability.
source: For example, E2 applied to hippocampal slices increases neuronal excitability (Teyler et al., 1980; Kumar and Foster, 2002; Carrer et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 potentiates excitatory synaptic transmission in hippocampal slices on a time scale of minutes.
source: potentiates excitatory synaptic transmission (Wong and Moss, 1992; Kramar et al., 2009; Smejkalova and Woolley, 2010; Oberlander and Woolley, 2016), and suppresses inhibitory synaptic transmission (Huang and Woolley, 2012; Tabatadze et al., 2015), on a time scale of minutes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 suppresses inhibitory synaptic transmission in hippocampal slices on a time scale of minutes.
source: potentiates excitatory synaptic transmission (Wong and Moss, 1992; Kramar et al., 2009; Smejkalova and Woolley, 2010; Oberlander and Woolley, 2016), and suppresses inhibitory synaptic transmission (Huang and Woolley, 2012; Tabatadze et al., 2015), on a time scale of minutes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Male and female rats were randomly assigned to receive vehicle or fadrozole.
source: Male (n=9) and female (n=12) rats were randomly assigned to receive vehicle or the selective aromatase inhibitor, fadrozole (Häusler et al., 1989a; 1989b; Browne et al., 1991)
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Fadrozole is a selective aromatase inhibitor.
source: the selective aromatase inhibitor, fadrozole (Häusler et al., 1989a; 1989b; Browne et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Rats were injected with KA (10 mg/kg, i.p.) to induce SE.
source: and were injected with KA (10 mg/kg, i.p.; Sperk et al., 1985) to induce SE.
evidence: This describes the experimental method with citation support.

claim: Vehicle or fadrozole (40 mg/kg) was administered through a tail vein catheter after seizures were detected in hippocampal EEG recordings.
source: After seizures were detected in hippocampal EEG recordings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), vehicle or fadrozole (40 mg/kg) was administered through a tail vein catheter, and seizures were recorded for an additional 2 hrs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Seizures detected prior to i.v. injections did not differ in latency, duration, amplitude, or β-low γ power in rats assigned to either treatment group.
source: Seizures detected prior to i.v. injections did not differ in latency, duration, amplitude, or β-low γ power in rats assigned to either treatment group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I.

claim: Vehicle-treated rats showed progression of seizure activity beginning with individual seizures that evolved to merging seizures.
source: Vehicle-treated rats showed the expected progression of seizure activity, beginning with individual seizures that evolved to merging seizures (Treiman et al., 1990) with high EEG amplitude and increased power.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to published literature.

claim: Fadrozole-treated rats showed much lower seizure activity, particularly during the 2nd hr when vehicle rats typically experienced merging seizures.
source: In contrast, fadrozole-treated rats showed much lower seizure activity, particularly during the 2nd hr when vehicle rats typically experienced merging seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The effects of fadrozole were the same in males and females.
source: The effects of fadrozole were the same in males and females (all p values >0.30) so data were combined.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The seizure-induced increase in EEG amplitude during the 2nd hr was 46% lower on average in fadrozole-treated compared to vehicle-treated rats.
source: The seizure-induced increase in EEG amplitude during the 2nd hr was 46% lower on average in fadrozole-treated compared to vehicle-treated rats (time x drug: F1,19=10.36, p<0.01, Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The time animals spent in seizures based on a 5x baseline threshold of EEG amplitude was 73% lower in the 2nd hr in fadrozole-treated rats.
source: and the time animals spent in seizures based on a 5x baseline threshold of EEG amplitude was 73% lower in the 2nd hr (time x drug: F1,19=20.88, p<0.001, Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fadrozole significantly attenuated the seizure-induced increase in EEG power in the δ-θ (1–10 Hz) frequency range over the entire 2 hr testing period.
source: In addition to EEG amplitude, fadrozole also significantly attenuated the seizure-induced increase in EEG power in the δ-θ (1–10 Hz, F1,19=21.50, p<0.001) and β-low γ (10–50 Hz, F1,19=8.08, p=0.01) frequency ranges over the entire 2 hr testing period (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Fadrozole significantly attenuated the seizure-induced increase in EEG power in the β-low γ (10–50 Hz) frequency range over the entire 2 hr testing period.
source: In addition to EEG amplitude, fadrozole also significantly attenuated the seizure-induced increase in EEG power in the δ-θ (1–10 Hz, F1,19=21.50, p<0.001) and β-low γ (10–50 Hz, F1,19=8.08, p=0.01) frequency ranges over the entire 2 hr testing period (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The seizure-induced increase in β-low γ power in fadrozole-treated rats was 59% lower during the 2nd hr.
source: The seizure-induced increase in β-low γ power in fadrozole-treated rats was 59% lower during the 2nd hr (Figure 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Time in seizure based on a threshold of 5x baseline β-low γ power was 44% lower in the 2nd hr in fadrozole-treated rats.
source: and time in seizure based on a threshold of 5x baseline β-low γ power was 44% lower in the 2nd hr (time x drug: F1,19=16.87, p<0.01, Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: KA seizures are characterized by stereotyped and progressively more severe seizure behaviors commonly identified using a Racine scale.
source: KA seizures are characterized by stereotyped and progressively more severe seizure behaviors commonly identified using a Racine scale (Racine, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The seizure behaviors that appear earliest (Racine 0–2) correspond with electrographic seizure activity in the hippocampus and reflect mild limbic seizures.
source: The seizure behaviors that appear earliest (Racine 0–2) correspond with electrographic seizure activity in the hippocampus (Figure 2B,C) and reflect mild limbic seizures
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C and citations.

claim: Later-occurring convulsive seizures (Racine 3–5) reflect both limbic and extra-limbic seizure activity.
source: in contrast to the later-occurring convulsive seizures (Racine 3–5), which reflect both limbic and extra-limbic seizure activity (Lothman and Collins, 1981; McIntyre et al., 1982; Lothman et al., 1989; Handforth and Ackermann, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Normalized hippocampal EEG amplitude is better correlated with behavioral signs of mild limbic seizures (Racine 0, 1–2) than convulsive seizures (Racine 3, 4, 5).
source: Cross-correlation between EEG and the occurrence of specific seizure behaviors for each rat confirmed that normalized hippocampal EEG amplitude (F4,86=30.22, p<0.001; Figure 2D) and power (F4,86=15.63, both p<0.001; Figure 2E) are better correlated with behavioral signs of mild limbic seizures (Racine 0, 1–2) than convulsive seizures (Racine 3, 4, 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Normalized hippocampal EEG power is better correlated with behavioral signs of mild limbic seizures (Racine 0, 1–2) than convulsive seizures (Racine 3, 4, 5).
source: Cross-correlation between EEG and the occurrence of specific seizure behaviors for each rat confirmed that normalized hippocampal EEG amplitude (F4,86=30.22, p<0.001; Figure 2D) and power (F4,86=15.63, both p<0.001; Figure 2E) are better correlated with behavioral signs of mild limbic seizures (Racine 0, 1–2) than convulsive seizures (Racine 3, 4, 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fadrozole decreased the strength of cross-correlation between EEG and some behaviors, particularly those reflecting convulsive seizures.
source: Interestingly, fadrozole decreased the strength of cross-correlation between EEG and some behaviors, particularly those reflecting convulsive seizures (Racine 3: amplitude: t18=2.87, power: t18=2.80, and Racine 4: power: t17=2.57, all p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Vehicle-treated rats spent progressively more time in seizure, peaking during the 2nd hr when they spent 47 ± 9% of time in seizures more severe than staring (Racine stages 1–5).
source: Behavioral seizures induced by KA followed a similar pattern as electrographic seizures in that vehicle-treated rats spent progressively more time in seizure, peaking during the 2nd hr when they spent 47 ± 9% of time in seizures more severe than staring (Racine stages 1–5, Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Fadrozole-treated rats spent only 16 ± 8% of time in Racine 1–5 seizures during the 2nd hr.
source: This progressive increase was largely absent in fadrozole-treated rats, who spent only 16 ± 8% of time in Racine 1–5 seizures during the 2nd hr (time x drug: F1,19=7.22, p<0.05, Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In fadrozole-treated rats, convulsive seizures (Racine 3–5) typically subsided within 2 hrs, such that fadrozole-treated rats spent only ~3% of time in convulsive seizures, compared to 12% in vehicle-treated rats.
source: Furthermore, in fadrozole-treated rats, convulsive seizures (Racine 3–5) typically subsided within 2 hrs, such that fadrozole-treated rats spent only ~3% of time in convulsive seizures, compared to 12% in vehicle-treated rats (time x drug: F1,19=6.59, p<0.05, Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Fadrozole significantly decreased the proportion of rats in behavioral SE at any point during 2 hrs of testing.
source: For example, fadrozole significantly decreased the proportion of rats in behavioral SE at any point during 2 hrs of testing (F1,19=7.66, p<0.05, Figure 2I)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Among rats that reached criteria for behavioral SE, the time spent in SE was significantly lower in fadrozole-treated animals.
source: and among rats that reached criteria for behavioral SE, the time spent in SE was also significantly lower in fadrozole-treated animals (Veh: 1296 ± 245 sec; Fad: 436 ± 141 sec, t14=2.26, p<0.05, not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Fadrozole significantly reduced the proportion of rats in electrographic SE during the 2nd hr.
source: Fadrozole also significantly reduced the proportion of rats in electrographic SE during the 2nd hr (F3,57=7.38, p<0.001, Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Probe recovery was 30.1 ± 2.9% of external E2 concentration recovered in dialysate.
source: After optimization, we obtained 30.1 ± 2.9% of external E2 concentration recovered in dialysate (i.e., probe recovery) with little difference between concentrations of E2 (31.3 ± 5.4% and 28.9 ± 3.6% for 0.25 and 1.0 ng/ml E2, respectively) or 1st and 2nd 30 min samples at each concentration (25.9 ± 2.1% and 31.8 ± 3.4%, respectively, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: E2 concentration in dialysate reached a stable level within 30 min.
source: The latter result indicates that E2 concentration in dialysate reached a stable level within 30 min.
evidence: This is an inference from the probe recovery data showing similar values in 1st and 2nd 30 min samples.

claim: Probe recovery was linear, evidenced by dialysate E2 concentration changing linearly with bath concentration.
source: Probe recovery was linear, evidenced by dialysate E2 concentration changing linearly with bath concentration (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Exogenously administered E2 (10 µg, s.c.) could be detected in the hippocampus within 30 min and then declined gradually over 2 hrs.
source: In vivo tests showed that exogenously administered E2 (10 µg, s.c.) could be detected in the hippocampus within 30 min and then declined gradually over 2 hrs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Retrodialysis of androstenedione (4-dione, 1 ng/ml) into the dorsal hippocampus produced a large increase in local E2 concentration (+8.9 ± 3.2 pg/ml or 310 ± 67% of baseline).
source: As shown in Figure 3E, 4-dione retrodialysis produced a large increase in local E2 concentration (+8.9 ± 3.2 pg/ml or 310 ± 67% of baseline; t9=3.15, p<0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The hippocampus can synthesize E2 in vivo.
source: demonstrating that the hippocampus can synthesize E2 in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 4-dione retrodialysis experiment showing increased E2 after androstenedione administration.

claim: The enzyme immunoassay used to measure E2 shows little to no cross-reactivity with steroids other than estrogens.
source: We confirmed that the enzyme immunoassay used to measure E2 (Remage-Healey et al., 2008) shows little to no cross-reactivity with steroids other than estrogens (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cross-reactivity of the E2 assay with 4-dione was 0.01% at 200 ng/ml.
source: Cross-reactivity with 4-dione was 0.01% at 200 ng/ml, so the 1 ng/ml 4-dione dose used for retrodialysis would not be detected in the assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation data.

claim: E2 levels in the hippocampus more than doubled during a 2 hr period after KA overall.
source: This showed that, overall, E2 levels in the hippocampus more than doubled during a 2 hr period after KA (F2,60=9.15, p<0.001, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of microdialysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mean basal concentration of E2 detected in dialysate was 6.3 ± 0.8 pg/ml (23.3 ± 2.9 pM).
source: The mean basal concentration of E2 we detected in dialysate was 6.3 ± 0.8 pg/ml (23.3 ± 2.9 pM)
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis experimental data.

claim: Basal E2 levels were slightly higher in females (7.1 ± 1.0 pg/ml) than in males (5.4 ± 1.2 pg/ml), but the difference was not statistically significant.
source: levels were slightly higher in females (7.1 ± 1.0 pg/ml) than in males (5.4 ± 1.2 pg/ml), but the difference was not statistically significant (t41=1.10. p=0.28).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of microdialysis data.

claim: The highest E2 concentrations measured were 16.7 pg/ml (61.3 pM) during baseline and 30.0 pg/ml (110.1 pM) after KA injection.
source: The highest E2 concentrations we measured were 16.7 pg/ml (61.3 pM) during baseline and 30.0 pg/ml (110.1 pM) after KA injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis experimental data.

claim: The seizure-induced increase in hippocampal E2 was similar in both sexes and hemispheres.
source: The seizure-induced increase in hippocampal E2 was similar in both sexes and hemispheres (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Animals with relatively mild seizures (<30 min) showed a small increase in E2 (188 ± 38% baseline) that was delayed relative to KA administration.
source: This demonstrated that animals with relatively mild seizures (<30 min, n=10, Figure 4B) showed a small increase in E2 (188 ± 38% baseline, F2,18=5.39, p<0.05) that was delayed relative to KA administration
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of microdialysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Animals with moderate seizures (30–90 min) showed a large increase in E2 (318 ± 68% baseline) evident within the first 30 min.
source: whereas those with moderate seizures (30–90 min, n=17, Figure 4C) showed a large increase in E2 (318 ± 68% baseline, F2,23=8.22, p<0.01) evident within the first 30 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of microdialysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Animals with very severe seizures (>90 min) began with significantly higher basal E2 (10.4 ± 2.0 pg/ml) than those with mild or moderate seizures (5.3 ± 0.8 pg/ml).
source: Interestingly, the small fraction of animals with very severe seizures (>90 min, n=4, Figure 4D) began with significantly higher basal E2 (10.4 ± 2.0 pg/ml) than those with mild or moderate seizures (5.3 ± 0.8 pg/ml, t29=2.22, p<0.05, Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of microdialysis data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Hippocampal E2 remained high during seizures in animals with very severe seizures (97 ± 33% baseline).
source: and hippocampal E2 remained high during seizures in those animals (97 ± 33% baseline).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis experimental data.

claim: In animals with mild or moderate seizures, E2 levels increased to 8.9 ± 0.8 pg/ml, a significant difference from their baseline.
source: This is in contrast to animals with mild or moderate seizures in which E2 levels increased to 8.9 ± 0.8 pg/ml, a significant difference from their baseline (t52=2.54, p<0.05, Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of microdialysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Fadrozole (10 µg/side) or vehicle was bilaterally infused into the dorsal hippocampus 20 min before KA (10 mg/kg, i.p.) and seizures were monitored for 2 hrs.
source: To test this possibility, we first bilaterally infused fadrozole (10 µg/side, n=10) or vehicle (30% β-cyclodextrin in saline, n=11) into the dorsal hippocampus 20 min before KA (10 mg/kg, i.p.) and monitored seizures for 2 hrs.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Intra-hippocampal fadrozole did not affect the strength of cross-correlation between EEG amplitude and seizure behaviors.
source: In contrast to systemic fadrozole, however, intra-hippocampal fadrozole did not affect the strength of cross-correlation between EEG amplitude (Figure 5C) or power (Figure 5D) and seizure behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Intra-hippocampal fadrozole did not affect the strength of cross-correlation between EEG power and seizure behaviors.
source: In contrast to systemic fadrozole, however, intra-hippocampal fadrozole did not affect the strength of cross-correlation between EEG amplitude (Figure 5C) or power (Figure 5D) and seizure behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Among rats that exhibited electrographic seizures, intra-hippocampal fadrozole significantly attenuated the seizure-related increase in β-low γ power.
source: Importantly, among rats that exhibited electrographic seizures, fadrozole significantly attenuated the seizure-related increase in β-low γ power (t19=2.43, p<0.05, Figure 5E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The effect of intra-hippocampal fadrozole was specific to the β-low γ frequency range; neither δ-θ (1–10 Hz) nor ripple (100–200 Hz) power showed significantly different seizure-related changes.
source: In contrast to systemic inhibition of aromatase with fadrozole (Figure 1), the effect of intra-hippocampal fadrozole was specific to the β-low γ frequency range; neither δ-θ (1–10 Hz) nor ripple (100–200 Hz) power showed significantly different seizure-related changes (p values >0.2, Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Time spent in seizures as detected by 5x baseline power in the β-low γ range was significantly reduced by intra-hippocampal fadrozole.
source: Time spent in seizures as detected by 5x baseline power in the β-low γ range was significantly reduced by intra-hippocampal fadrozole, however (t19=2.62, p<0.05; Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: Brain injury can induce aromatase expression in glia.
source: For example, previous studies have shown that brain injury can induce aromatase expression in glia (Peterson et al., 2001; Carswell et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Intra-hippocampal fadrozole (10 µg/side) significantly delayed the onset of behavioral seizures (Racine 0).
source: This showed that fadrozole significantly delayed the onset of behavioral seizures (Racine 0, t52=2.57, p<0.05, Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Significantly fewer fadrozole-treated rats progressed beyond staring and the majority never progressed beyond mild limbic seizures.
source: While the proportion of rats exhibiting the earliest stage of behavioral seizure, staring (Racine 0), was the same in vehicle- and fadrozole-infused animals, significantly fewer fadrozole-treated rats progressed beyond staring and the majority never progressed beyond mild limbic seizures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In vehicle-treated rats, roughly 2/3 progressed to convulsive seizures.
source: This was in contrast to vehicle-treated rats in which roughly 2/3 progressed to convulsive seizures (χ2-tests, p<0.05 or p<0.01, Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Among rats that progressed to more severe seizure behaviors, intra-hippocampal fadrozole significantly reduced the time animals spent in any seizures beyond staring (Racine 1–5) in the 2nd hr.
source: In addition, even among rats that progressed to more severe seizure behaviors, fadrozole significantly reduced the time animals spent in any seizures beyond staring (Racine 1–5, time x drug: F1,30=6.99, p<0.05; Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Among rats that progressed to more severe seizure behaviors, intra-hippocampal fadrozole significantly reduced the time animals spent in mild limbic seizures specifically (Racine 1–2) in the 2nd hr.
source: and in mild limbic seizures specifically (Racine 1–2, time x drug: F1,30=5.64, p<0.05, Figure 6D) in the 2nd hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was no effect of intra-hippocampal fadrozole on the density of Fluoro-Jade B-positive cells in any hippocampal subregion.
source: This showed no differences between vehicle- and fadrozole-treated animals (t21<0.45, p>0.66, for all subregions, Figure 6—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acute aromatase inhibition does not exacerbate seizure-induced cell death.
source: demonstrating that acute aromatase inhibition does not exacerbate seizure-induced cell death.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Fluoro-Jade B staining data.

claim: Behavioral seizures were more severe with gonads intact, consistent with a proconvulsant effect of circulating hormones.
source: Overall, behavioral seizures were more severe with gonads intact, consistent with a proconvulsant effect of circulating hormones (Terasawa and Timiras, 1968; Nicoletti et al., 1985; Woolley, 2000; Mejias-Aponte et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to published literature.

claim: The dose of KA was lowered to 7.5 mg/kg in gonadally intact females to achieve the same range of seizure severity as in males treated with 10 mg/kg KA.
source: This was particularly evident in females, in which it was not feasible to use 10 mg/kg KA. Thus we lowered the dose of KA to 7.5 mg/kg in females (n=5 vehicle, n=4 letrozole), to achieve the same range of seizure severity as in males treated with 10 mg/kg KA (n=6 vehicle, n=6 letrozole).
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Letrozole significantly reduced the seizure-related increase in EEG amplitude, by 40%, throughout all 6 hrs of recording.
source: Analysis of these seizures showed that letrozole significantly reduced the seizure-related increase in EEG amplitude, by 40% (F1,18=6.63, p<0.05, Figure 7D)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Letrozole decreased the time spent in seizures based on a 5x baseline threshold of EEG amplitude, by 61%, throughout all 6 hrs of recording.
source: and decreased the time spent in seizures based on a 5x baseline threshold of EEG amplitude, by 61% (F1,18=4.75, p<0.05, Figure 7E), throughout all 6 hrs of recording.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Letrozole attenuated the seizure-induced increase in power across all 6 hrs of recording, with significant effects in the δ-θ and β-low γ ranges.
source: Examination of changes in EEG power in 2 hr epochs (Figure 7F) showed that letrozole also attenuated the seizure-induced increase in power across all 6 hrs of recording. The effect of letrozole was statistically significant in the δ-θ (F1,18=4.56, p<0.05) and β-low γ ranges (F1,18=5.54, p<0.05) but not in the ripple range (F1,18=2.82, p=0.11) (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7F and 7H.

claim: Time spent in seizures as assessed by a 5x baseline increase in power in β-low γ range was significantly lower in rats treated with letrozole.
source: Time spent in seizures as assessed by a 5x baseline increase in power in β-low γ range was also significantly lower in rats treated with letrozole (F1,18=8.15, p<0.05, not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The proportion of rats in behavioral SE was significantly lower in letrozole- than vehicle-treated animals throughout 6 hrs of testing.
source: The proportion of rats in behavioral SE was significantly lower in letrozole- than vehicle-treated animals throughout 6 hrs of testing (F1,18=5.13, p<0.05, Figure 8C)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The proportion of rats in electrographic SE was significantly lower in letrozole- than vehicle-treated animals.
source: as was the proportion of rats in electrographic SE (F1,18=7.85, p<0.05, Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Gonadally intact males spent twofold more time in Racine 1–5 seizures in the first 2 hrs after KA than gonadectomized males did.
source: Intact males spent twofold more time in Racine 1–5 seizures in the first 2 hrs after KA than gonadectomized males did (F1,9=15.67, p<0.01, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Behavioral seizures began much more quickly in gonadally intact males than in gonadectomized males.
source: Behavioral seizures also began much more quickly in gonadally intact males. Racine 1–2 seizures began within 231 ± 112 s in intact males compared to 3193 ± 1251 s in gonadectomized males (t9=2.61, p<0.05)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: All 6 intact males reached Racine 3–5 seizures within 1 hr after KA whereas only 1 of 5 gonadectomized males did.
source: and all 6 intact males reached Racine 3–5 seizures within 1 hr after KA whereas only 1 of 5 gonadectomized males did (χ 2=7.54, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The difference between gonadectomized and intact males in behavioral seizures was not evident in EEG recordings.
source: Interestingly, while the difference between gonadectomized and intact males was very clear in behavioral seizures, this difference was not evident in EEG recordings. For example, normalized EEG amplitude increased after KA with a similar time course in both groups (p>0.50, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There was no effect of systemic letrozole on the density of Fluoro-Jade B-positive cells in any hippocampal subregion.
source: Counts of Fluoro-Jade B-positive cells showed no significant differences between vehicle and letrozole groups in any hippocampal subregion examined (p>0.19, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of histological data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The 4 of 6 letrozole-treated rats that did not experience electrographic SE during testing had significantly fewer Fluoro-Jade B-positive cells in CA3 than the 2 of 6 letrozole-treated and all 6 vehicle-treated rats that did reach SE.
source: The degree of cell death evident in CA3 was most closely related to seizure severity in that the 4 of 6 letrozole-treated rats that did not experience electrographic SE during testing had significantly fewer Fluoro-Jade B-positive cells in CA3 than the 2 of 6 letrozole-treated and all 6 vehicle-treated rats that did reach SE (t10=2.36, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of histological data.

claim: E2 application to hippocampal slices rapidly increases extracellularly recorded field potentials.
source: Since the early work of Teyler et al. (1980), which showed that E2 application to hippocampal slices rapidly increases extracellularly recorded field potentials
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: E2 suppresses Ca++-activated K+ currents to reduce the slow afterhyperpolarization following a burst of action potentials.
source: For example, E2 suppresses Ca++-activated K+ currents to reduce the slow afterhyperpolarization following a burst of action potentials (Kumar and Foster, 2002; Carrer et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2 increases repetitive action potential firing in response to current injection.
source: and increases repetitive action potential firing in response to current injection (Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: E2 acutely promotes excitatory synaptic transmission through both increased glutamate release probability and increased postsynaptic sensitivity to glutamate.
source: E2 also acutely promotes excitatory synaptic transmission through both increased glutamate release probability and increased postsynaptic sensitivity to glutamate (Kramar et al., 2009; Smejkalova and Woolley, 2010; Oberlander and Woolley, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2's acute actions are mediated by membrane-associated forms of the classical estrogen receptors, ERα and ERβ.
source: Most studies indicate that E2's acute actions are mediated by membrane-associated forms of the classical estrogen receptors, ERα (Huang and Woolley, 2012; Tabatadze et al., 2015) and ERβ (Kramar et al., 2009; Smejkalova and Woolley, 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2's acute actions are mediated by the G protein-coupled ER, GPER1.
source: as well as the G protein-coupled ER, GPER1 (Kumar et al., 2015; Oberlander and Woolley, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: E2's acute actions involve downstream signaling through protein kinases including Src, Erk1/2, protein kinase A, and RhoA kinase to influence synaptic transmission.
source: and involve downstream signaling through protein kinases including Src, Erk1/2, protein kinase A, and RhoA kinase (Boulware et al., 2005; Kramar et al., 2009; Zadran et al., 2009) to influence synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Basal E2 concentrations in the hippocampus of gonadectomized rats average at least ~20 pg/ml (74 pM).
source: For example, based on our probe recovery estimate of ~30% and the mean basal concentrations of E2 we detected in dialysate, basal E2 concentrations in the hippocampus of gonadectomized rats average at least ~20 pg/ml (74 pM).
evidence: This is calculated from the microdialysis data and probe recovery measurements.

claim: Hippocampal E2 reaches ~100 pg/ml (367 pM) after KA.
source: The highest concentrations we measured indicate that hippocampal E2 reaches ~100 pg/ml (367 pM) after KA
evidence: This is calculated from the microdialysis data and probe recovery measurements.

claim: Aromatase is concentrated at synapses based on electron microscopic immunogold labeling.
source: First, electron microscopic immunogold labeling indicates that aromatase is concentrated at synapses (Hojo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The aromatase enzyme can switch between aromatase and hydroxylase activity in a pH-dependent manner in peripheral systems.
source: Studies in peripheral systems show that the aromatase enzyme can switch between aromatase and hydroxylase activity in a pH-dependent manner (Osawa et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The ratio of aromatase to hydroxylase activity is greatest at acidic pH, whereas hydroxylase activity predominates at alkaline pH.
source: The ratio of aromatase to hydroxylase activity is greatest at acidic pH, whereas hydroxylase activity predominates at alkaline pH.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about aromatase enzyme activity.

claim: KCl-induced depolarization of neurons produces biphasic changes in intracellular pH: an initial acid transient is followed by alkalinization.
source: This is potentially relevant to seizures in that, in vitro, KCl-induced depolarization of neurons (Svichar et al., 2011) or treatment with the NMDA receptor co-agonist glycine (Diering et al., 2011) produces biphasic changes in intracellular pH: an initial acid transient is followed by alkalinization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Glutamate retrodialysis reduced E2 levels in a cortical brain area in zebra finches.
source: For example, glutamate retrodialysis reduced E2 levels in a cortical brain area in zebra finches (Remage-Healey et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Treatment of quail hypothalamic explants with glutamate receptor agonists lowered aromatase activity.
source: and treatment of quail hypothalamic explants with glutamate receptor agonists lowered aromatase activity (Balthazart et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Glutamate receptor activation increases aromatase activity in rat hippocampal slices.
source: In contrast, glutamate receptor activation increases aromatase activity in rat hippocampal slices (Hojo et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Species differences in aromatase enzyme structure may lead to differences in aromatase regulation.
source: One possibility is that species differences in enzyme structure lead to differences in aromatase regulation. Aromatase activity requires access to lipophilic substrate, and differences between avian and mammalian aromatase are greater in a region responsible for membrane association (~58% identity) than catalytic activity (~73% identity, chicken vs. rat, Ghosh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural differences in aromatase between species.

claim: Stress regulates enzymes involved in E2 metabolism in the avian brain.
source: For example, studies in the avian brain indicate that stress regulates enzymes involved in E2 metabolism (Soma et al., 2004; Dickens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Longer-term treatment with E2 is neuroprotective, including in the KA seizure model.
source: Longer-term treatment with E2 is known to be neuroprotective, including in the KA seizure model (Hoffman et al., 2003; Schauwecker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All animal procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
source: All animal procedures were performed in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals and were approved by the Northwestern University Animal Care and Use Committee (Animal Study Protocol: IS00000520, Animal Welfare Assurance: A3283-01).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Young adult male and female Sprague-Dawley rats (~50 days old) were used in the experiments.
source: Young adult male and female Sprague-Dawley rats (~50 days old, Harlan, Indianapolis, IN) were gonadectomized or gonadally intact, and were implanted with either unilateral microdialysis guide cannulae (CMA, Kista, Sweden) or bilateral intra-hippocampal infusion guide cannulae (PlasticsOne, Roanoke, VA).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and methods.

claim: Previous studies have reported no estrous cycle-related differences in the occurrence of acute KA-induced SE.
source: Previous studies have reported no estrous cycle-related differences in the occurrence of acute KA-induced SE (D'Amour et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: No estrous cycle-related differences in seizures were found in this study.
source: and we also found no differences related to the estrous cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The standard dose of KA (10 mg/kg) was used for all experiments with EEG recording, except in gonadally intact females, in which KA was lowered to 7.5 mg/kg.
source: The standard dose of KA (10 mg/kg, Sperk et al., 1985) was used for all experiments with EEG recording, except in gonadally intact females, in which KA was lowered to 7.5 mg/kg because 10 mg/kg in intact females resulted in very severe seizures in a pilot study.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods with citation support.

claim: For the experiment without EEG recording, the dose of KA was increased to 15 mg/kg to achieve the same range of seizure severity as in animals with EEG electrodes implanted.
source: For the experiment without EEG recording, the dose was increased to 15 mg/kg to achieve the same range of seizure severity as in animals with EEG electrodes implanted.
evidence: This describes the experimental rationale.

claim: Animals with microdialysis experienced more severe seizures than rats without microdialysis, possibly due to tissue damage from microdialysis probes.
source: For the dialysis experiments, 1.25–5 mg/kg doses were used, as these animals experienced more severe seizures than rats without microdialysis, possibly due to tissue damage from microdialysis probes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments with speculation about the cause.

claim: The dose of fadrozole (40 mg/kg) was chosen based on previous studies and results of a pilot study.
source: The dose of fadrozole was chosen based on previous studies (Wade et al., 1994; Taziaux et al., 2007) and results of a pilot study (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale with citation support.

claim: β-low γ (10–50 Hz) power is known to be sensitive to KA both in vitro and in vivo.
source: We focused further analyses on β-low γ power because this is known to be sensitive to KA both in vitro (Fisahn et al., 2004) and in vivo (Medvedev et al., 2000; Lévesque et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: β-low γ power may contribute to the spread of seizures to other brain regions.
source: and may contribute to the spread of seizures to other brain regions (Finnerty and Jefferys, 2000; Lévesque et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fadrozole is a potent and specific non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor.
source: Fadrozole is a potent and specific non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor (Häusler et al., 1989a; 1989b; Browne et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fadrozole has been used previously to study how chronic aromatase inhibition influences male sex behavior and affective behaviors.
source: that has been used previously to study how chronic aromatase inhibition influences male sex behavior (Vagell and McGinnis, 1997; Huddleston et al., 2006) and affective behaviors (Graham and Milad, 2014; Carrier et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The enzyme immunoassay used has little to no cross-reactivity with non-estrogens.
source: These results showed that the EIA used has little to no cross-reactivity with non-estrogens.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the cross-reactivity testing experiments.
